claim: Replisome assembly requires the loading of replicative hexameric helicases onto origins by AAA+ ATPases.
source: Replisome assembly requires the loading of replicative hexameric helicases onto origins by AAA+ ATPases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about replisome assembly mechanisms.

claim: The phage 77 ORF104 protein binds directly to the Staphylococcus aureus replicative helicase loader, DnaI.
source: a small, 52 amino acid protein from phage strain 77, encoded by the ORF104 gene, has been reported to interact directly with the Staphylococcus aureus helicase loader, DnaI
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2004 and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The phage 77 ORF104 protein inhibits host DNA replication in vivo.
source: a small, 52 amino acid protein from phage strain 77, encoded by the ORF104 gene, has been reported to interact directly with the Staphylococcus aureus helicase loader, DnaI, and to inhibit host DNA replication in vivo (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by Liu et al., 2004.

claim: The discovery of 77ORF104 marks the first known instance in which the replication initiation machinery of a bacterium can be inhibited by an exogenous factor.
source: The discovery of 77ORF104 marks the first known instance in which the replication initiation machinery of a bacterium can be inhibited by an exogenous factor (Liu et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2004.

claim: The phage 77 ORF104 protein binds to the AAA+ ATPase domain of SaDnaI.
source: We show that the phage protein binds directly to DnaI's AAA+ ATPase domain
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript, including pull-down assays and crystal structures.

claim: 77ORF104 binding remodels a region critical for loader self-assembly.
source: We show that the phage protein binds directly to DnaI's AAA+ ATPase domain, where it both remodels a region critical for loader self-assembly
evidence: Supported by structural data showing conformational changes in the ISM region.

claim: 77ORF104 sterically masks a known loader-loader interaction site.
source: We show that the phage protein binds directly to DnaI's AAA+ ATPase domain, where it both remodels a region critical for loader self-assembly and sterically masks a known loader-loader interaction site.
evidence: Supported by structural superposition data showing steric clash with neighboring protomers.

claim: 77ORF104 binding represses the helicase loader's ATP hydrolysis activity.
source: Inhibitor binding, which represses the helicase loader's ATP hydrolysis activity
evidence: Supported by radioactive ATP hydrolysis assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bacterial helicase loaders possess an auto-regulatory element located within their variable linker region that serves to help restrict premature loader self-assembly.
source: our data not only establish a new means by which viruses can inhibit DNA replication, but also indicate that bacterial helicase loaders possess an unanticipated auto-regulatory element, located within their variable linker region, that serves to help restrict premature loader self-assembly.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis showing the linker occupies the same binding site as the inhibitor.

claim: 77ORF104 associates with SaDnaI in amylose pull-down assays.
source: By performing amylose pull-down assays using the tagged inhibitor protein as bait and DnaI as prey (Figure 1B), we confirmed that 77ORF104 associates with SaDnaI as previously reported (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Liu et al., 2004.

claim: Limited proteolysis of SaDnaI in the presence of 77ORF104 protects a distinct 20kDa species from digestion.
source: Inspection of the reactions using SDS-PAGE showed relatively rapid degradation of SaDnaI when the phage protein was omitted. By contrast, when 77ORF104 was added to the full-length loader, a distinct 20kDa species remained protected from digestion (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 77ORF104 binds to the isolated C-terminal AAA+ ATPase domain of SaDnaI but not to the N-terminal domain.
source: we found that the phage protein was capable of retaining both the isolated C-terminal AAA+ ATPase domain (with or without the preceding linker region) but not the N-terminal domain on its own (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: ATP is dispensable for the association of 77ORF104 with full-length SaDnaI.
source: ATP was found to be dispensable for association with the full-length loader (compare Figures 1B, 2C).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data comparing conditions with and without ATP.

claim: The interaction of 77ORF104 with SaDnaI is independent of nucleotide.
source: Together, these findings establish that the phage inhibitor binds directly to the ATPase fold of DnaI but that this interaction is independent of nucleotide.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assays performed with and without ATP.

claim: The apparent Kd for the 77ORF104-SaDnaIAAA+ interaction is 49 nM ± 19 nM.
source: The calculated apparent Kd (Kd, app = 49 nM ± 19 nM) for the inhibitor-loader AAA+ domain interaction proved comparable to that previously reported for the 77ORF104 protein and full-length SaDnaI (Kd = ~50 nM as reported by surface plasmon resonance) (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy binding assays and comparison to prior work.

claim: A crystal structure of the AAA+ domain of SaDnaI bound to both 77ORF104 and ADP•BeF3 was determined at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: we determined a crystal structure of the AAA+ domain of SaDnaI bound to both 77ORF104 and an ATP-mimetic, ADP•BeF3 (Figure 3A), using single-wavelength anomalous dispersion for phasing.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The final model of the ADP•BeF3-SaDnaIAAA+•77ORF104 complex converged at an Rwork/Rfree of 18.0%/21.8%.
source: Following several rounds of building and refinement, the model converged at an Rwork/Rfree of 18.0%/21.8% for the resolution range of 47.4–1.9 Å (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic refinement statistics.

claim: The final model of the ADP•BeF3-SaDnaIAAA+•77ORF104 complex contains residues 136–300 for SaDnaI and all 52 residues of 77ORF104.
source: The final model contains residues 136–300 for SaDnaI and all 52 residues of 77ORF104, and displays good overall stereochemistry.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic model building.

claim: 77ORF104 binds to SaDnaI in a 1:1 manner.
source: Examination of the ADP•BeF3-bound SaDnaIAAA+•77ORF104 complex revealed that the phage protein binds to the AAA+ domain of SaDnaI in a 1:1 manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SaDnaI's core AAA+ domain forms an αβα fold typical of the AAA+ superfamily.
source: SaDnaI's core AAA+ domain forms an αβα fold typical of the superfamily, and possesses all of the canonical motifs involved in nucleotide binding, such as the Walker-A, Walker-B and Sensor-I elements (Walker et al., 1982) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by structural data and comparison to known AAA+ structures.

claim: Lys39 of 77ORF104 projects into the SaDnaIAAA+ active site to engage the BeF3 moiety directly.
source: Lys39 of the phage inhibitor protein makes one of the more notable contacts, projecting into the SaDnaIAAA+ active site to engage the BeF3 moiety directly (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 77ORF104K39E mutant shows only a modest reduction in binding potency relative to wild-type protein.
source: Testing of the 77ORF104K39E mutant revealed only a modest reduction in potency relative to the wild-type protein, indicating that this amino acid serves a relatively peripheral role in stabilizing the inhibitor-loader interface (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by competition-based fluorescence anisotropy assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Removal of the C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 completely abrogates the ability of 77ORF104 to compete for binding by labeled inhibitor protein.
source: removal of the C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 or mutation of Tyr17 to glutamate completely abrogated the ability of 77ORF104 to compete for binding by the labeled inhibitor protein (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation of Tyr17 to glutamate in 77ORF104 completely abrogates the ability of 77ORF104 to compete for binding by labeled inhibitor protein.
source: removal of the C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 or mutation of Tyr17 to glutamate completely abrogated the ability of 77ORF104 to compete for binding by the labeled inhibitor protein (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tyr17 and the last five residues of the C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 are critical for the activity of the phage inhibitor.
source: Together, these data corroborate the structural interactions seen in the 77ORF104•SaDnaIAAA+ complex, demonstrating that both Tyr17 and the last five residues of the C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 are particularly critical for the activity of the phage inhibitor.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis and competition assay data.

claim: 77ORF104 occupies the same location as a neighboring protomer in AAA+ oligomers.
source: superposition of the SaDnaI AAA+ domain in our complex onto the AAA+ domain of a single subunit from a nucleotide-assembled dimer of Aquifex aeolicus DnaC (Mott et al., 2008) shows that the 77ORF104 protein occupies the same location as that of the neighboring protomer (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The phage inhibitor blocks SaDnaI activity by sterically blocking loader self-assembly.
source: This arrangement indicates that the phage inhibitor blocks SaDnaI activity by sterically blocking loader self-assembly.
evidence: Inferred from structural superposition showing steric clash.

claim: 77ORF104 induces a conformational change in the SaDnaI ISM, causing one of the α-helices to bend.
source: Inspection of this region, however, revealed that one of the α-helices of the SaDnaI ISM is bent compared to the ISM region of other helicase loaders (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The bent conformational change in the SaDnaI ISM is a consequence of 77ORF104 binding, not a species-specific state of the loader alone.
source: Structural alignment of the apo and 77ORF104-bound SaDnaIAAA+ models shows that the ISM is straight in the absence of the inhibitor, as seen in other helicase loader structures, such as Streptococcus pyogenes DnaI (shown in Figure 4B). This result indicates that the bent conformational change visualized for the SaDnaI ISM in the presence of the inhibitor is a consequence of 77ORF104 binding, rather than a species-specific state of the loader alone.
evidence: Supported by comparison of apo and inhibitor-bound structures.

claim: 77ORF104 does not disrupt the ability of DnaI to associate with the SaDnaC helicase.
source: Analysis of the reactions by SDS-PAGE revealed that both free SaDnaI and 77ORF104-bound SaDnaI were able to bind to the SaDnaC helicase equally well. By contrast, 77ORF104 did not bind to the SaDnaC helicase alone.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 77ORF104 inhibits SaDnaI function by preventing loader self-assembly rather than by blocking loader/helicase associations.
source: Overall, this result is consistent with a model in which 77ORF104 inhibits SaDnaI function not by blocking loader/helicase associations, but by preventing loader self-assembly.
evidence: Inferred from pull-down and light-scattering data.

claim: M13-ssDNA markedly stimulates ATP hydrolysis by SaDnaI.
source: Although SaDnaI was found to exhibit relatively modest ATPase activity on its own, the presence of M13-ssDNA markedly stimulated nucleotide turnover (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by radioactive ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 77ORF104 reduces the ssDNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis activity of SaDnaI.
source: when incubated with the 77ORF104 inhibitor in the presence of M13-ssDNA, the observed stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by ssDNA was much reduced (Figures 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Walker A mutant (K170A) of SaDnaI shows reduced ATP hydrolysis activity in the presence of ssDNA.
source: Both a Walker A mutant (K170A) and an arginine finger mutant (R288A) showed reduced ATP hydrolysis activity in the presence of ssDNA, indicating that the ssDNA-stimulated activity seen in our assays was indeed specific to DnaI and did not arise from a contaminating ATPase (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Arginine finger mutant (R288A) of SaDnaI shows reduced ATP hydrolysis activity in the presence of ssDNA.
source: Both a Walker A mutant (K170A) and an arginine finger mutant (R288A) showed reduced ATP hydrolysis activity in the presence of ssDNA, indicating that the ssDNA-stimulated activity seen in our assays was indeed specific to DnaI and did not arise from a contaminating ATPase (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The phage 77 ORF013 gene encodes a putative DnaC/DnaI-type helicase loader.
source: To determine the protein family to which 77ORF013 belongs, we searched the database for homologous proteins of known function. Surprisingly, this analysis revealed that the 77ORF013 gene encodes a putative DnaC/DnaI-type helicase loader (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The phage 77 ORF013 protein binds to the SaDnaC replicative helicase.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of different pull-down fractions showed that the phage 77 ORF013 protein was indeed capable of binding the SaDnaC replicative helicase (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 77ORF104 does not associate with the phage-encoded 77ORF013 helicase loader.
source: To address this question, we performed pull-downs of the purified tagged 77ORF104 inhibitor with 77ORF013. This assay revealed no association between the putative phage-encoded helicase loader and 77ORF104 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 77ORF104 does not interact with E. coli DnaC.
source: As measured by anisotropy, 77ORF104 also proved unable to interact with either a Gram-negative, DnaC-type helicase loader (E. coli DnaC) or 77ORF013 (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The association of 77ORF104 with DnaI is specific to the S. aureus helicase loader.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the phage inhibitor protein's association with SaDnaI is specific for binding only to the helicase loader of a host bacterium targeted by the virus.
evidence: Inferred from binding specificity data showing no interaction with E. coli DnaC or phage 77ORF013.

claim: 77ORF013 and 77ORF104 share a common operon in the phage 77 genome.
source: The two genes are located in the same operon in the phage chromosome, suggesting that they might be expressed contemporaneously and function synergistically.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis of phage 77.

claim: The 77ORF013 and 77ORF104 system may serve as a two-pronged mechanism by which host replication can be inhibited and a portion of the cell's replication machinery co-opted for promoting viral DNA duplication.
source: These observations suggest that the 77ORF013 and 77ORF104, which appear to both share a common operon, may serve as a two-pronged mechanism by which host replication can be inhibited and a portion of the cell's replication machinery co-opted for promoting viral DNA duplication.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings that 77ORF104 inhibits host loader and 77ORF013 binds host helicase.

claim: Homologs of both phage 77 ORF013 and ORF104 exist in other S. aureus phages such as phages 80 and 80α.
source: Surveys of other S. aureus phage genomes, such as phages 80 and 80α, reveal the existence of homologs of both the phage 77 ORF013 protein and the ORF104 inhibitor (Kwan et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2004; Tormo-Más et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to genomic surveys of other phages.

claim: The phage 77 ORF013/ORF104 system may be widespread among Staphylococcus aureus phages.
source: Surveys of other S. aureus phage genomes, such as phages 80 and 80α, reveal the existence of homologs of both the phage 77 ORF013 protein and the ORF104 inhibitor (Kwan et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2004; Tormo-Más et al., 2010), indicating that the phage 77 ORF013/ORF104 system may be widespread among Staphylococcus aureus phages.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of homologs in multiple S. aureus phages.

claim: The hijacking of a host replicative helicase for viral replication has been seen before with divergent viruses, including phages λ, P2 and Mu, as well as influenza.
source: The hijacking of a host replicative helicase for viral replication has been seen before with divergent viruses, including the phages λ, P2 and Mu, as well as influenza (Kawaguchi and Nagata, 2007; Kruklitis and Nakai, 1994; Mallory et al., 1990; Odegrip et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on viral hijacking mechanisms.

claim: The co-expression of a putative viral helicase loader with an inhibitor of a host helicase loader has only been seen for phage 77 and its relatives.
source: However, the co-expression of a putative viral helicase loader with an inhibitor of a host helicase loader has only been seen thus far for phage 77 and its relatives.
evidence: Based on comparison to known viral hijacking mechanisms.

claim: The C-terminal tail of 77ORF104 occupies a pocket that corresponds to the observed binding site for a portion of the DnaI linker region.
source: Superposition of the 77ORF104-SaDnaI complex with structures of other DnaI orthologs, particularly those that contain a portion of the helicase loaders' linker regions, reveal that the C-terminal tail of the inhibitor actually occupies a pocket that corresponds to the observed binding site for a portion of the linker itself (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The inter-domain linker of DnaI blocks a portion of the surface where subunit-subunit interactions form during loader self-association.
source: inspection of these overlays shows that in associating with its own AAA+ ATPase domain, the inter-domain linker additionally blocks a portion of the surface where subunit-subunit interactions form during loader self-association (Figure 7A, see inset).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7A inset.

claim: The linker of DnaI likely serves as a switch that reports on relative status of the N- and C-terminal regions, repressing loader-loader interactions until the correct helicase and DNA targets are bound.
source: This observation explains why DnaI ATPase domain constructs containing a portion of the linker crystallized as monomers even in the presence of nucleotide, and indicates that the linker likely serves as a switch that reports on relative status of the N- and C-terminal regions, repressing loader-loader interactions until the correct helicase and DNA targets are bound (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inferred from structural observations and crystallization behavior.

claim: The 77ORF104 protein exploits the linker-binding pocket to inactivate the host loader.
source: In this regard, the 77ORF104 protein exploits this binding locus, taking advantage of the linker-binding pocket to inactivate the host loader, an activity that would allow the cellular replicative helicase to be re-routed by the phage-encoded loader to promote viral replication (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: The linker-binding region of the DnaI AAA+ domain could serve as an attractive site for the development of chemical inhibitors to target helicase loading and DNA replication in bacteria.
source: This interaction, which occurs within a small hydrophobic pocket on the loader AAA+ ATPase domain, suggests that the linker-binding region of the DnaI AAA+ domain could serve as an attractive site for the development of chemical inhibitors to target helicase loading and DNA replication in bacteria.
evidence: Speculative statement based on structural findings.

claim: All cells face the challenging task of copying and passing on genetic information to progeny in an error-free manner as possible.
source: All cells face the challenging task of copying and passing on genetic information to progeny in an error-free manner as possible (Fuchs and Fujii, 2013 ; Sutera and Lovett, 2006).
evidence: General statement about cellular biology supported by citations.

claim: DNA synthesis is carried out by large, multi-subunit assemblies termed replisomes.
source: DNA synthesis is carried out by large, multi-subunit assemblies, termed replisomes, which are assembled at replication origins in accord with cell cycle cues.
evidence: Established knowledge about DNA replication.

claim: Initiator proteins play an essential role in selecting replication start sites, remodeling origin DNA, and recruiting replicative helicases to origins.
source: Dedicated proteins known as initiators play an essential role in selecting replication start sites, remodeling origin DNA, and providing an appropriate platform for recruiting replicative helicases to origins prior to the onset of strand synthesis (Costa et al., 2013; Dutta and Bell, 1997; Kaguni, 2011; Leonard and Grimwade, 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: All domains of life rely on replication initiation factors belonging to the AAA+ superfamily of nucleotide hydrolases.
source: Although specific helicase loading mechanisms vary across the three domains of life – archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes – all appear to rely on replication initiation factors belonging to the AAA+ (ATPases Associated with various cellular Activities) superfamily of nucleotide hydrolases.
evidence: General statement about conserved mechanisms across life.

claim: In bacteria, replication initiation relies on the DnaA initiator, which recognizes and marks the bacterial replication origin.
source: In bacteria, replication initiation relies on the DnaA initiator, which recognizes and marks the bacterial replication origin (Bramhill and Kornberg, 1988a; 1988b; Funnell et al., 1987; Hsu et al., 1994).
evidence: Established knowledge about bacterial replication supported by citations.

claim: DnaA actively opens an AT-rich region of the origin termed a DNA-unwinding element (DUE).
source: During initiation, DnaA actively opens an AT-rich region of the origin (Bramhill and Kornberg, 1988a, 1988b; Dixon and Kornberg, 1984; Funnell et al., 1987; Gille and Messer, 1991; Hsu et al., 1994; Skarstad et al., 1990), termed a DNA-unwinding element (DUE) (Kowalski and Eddy, 1989)
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: DnaA helps to recruit two copies of the replicative helicase to the newly melted single strands.
source: During initiation, DnaA actively opens an AT-rich region of the origin (Bramhill and Kornberg, 1988a, 1988b; Dixon and Kornberg, 1984; Funnell et al., 1987; Gille and Messer, 1991; Hsu et al., 1994; Skarstad et al., 1990), termed a DNA-unwinding element (DUE) (Kowalski and Eddy, 1989), and helps to recruit two copies of the replicative helicase to the newly melted single strands.
evidence: Established knowledge about bacterial replication initiation.

claim: In certain Gram-negative bacteria, a protein known as DnaC assists with loading of the helicase (known in these organisms as DnaB).
source: In certain Gram-negative bacteria, a protein known as DnaC assists with loading of the helicase (known in these organisms as DnaB)
evidence: Established knowledge about bacterial helicase loading.

claim: Many Gram-positive species retain a homolog of DnaC termed DnaI.
source: many Gram-positive species retain a homolog of DnaC termed DnaI.
evidence: Established knowledge about bacterial helicase loaders.

claim: Both DnaC and DnaI are composed of an N-terminal helicase binding domain that connects to a C-terminal AAA+ ATPase domain by a variable linker region of unknown function.
source: Both DnaC and DnaI are composed of an N-terminal helicase binding domain that connects to a C-terminal AAA+ ATPase domain by a variable linker region of unknown function (Loscha et al., 2009) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Established knowledge about DnaC/I structure supported by citation.

claim: There is evidence that ATPase activity by DnaC/I proteins controls key aspects of the helicase loading cycle and may be auto-regulated.
source: There is evidence that ATPase activity by DnaC/I proteins controls key aspects of the helicase loading cycle and may be auto-regulated (Davey et al., 2002; Ioannou et al., 2006; Learn et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanism by which DnaC/I ATPase activity is controlled is not understood.
source: however, the mechanism by which this control is exerted is not understood.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: There is renewed interest in exploring bacteriophage genomes to discover new antimicrobial agents due to the rise in multi-drug resistant bacterial strains.
source: Given the marked rise in multi-drug resistant bacterial strains, along with associated human fatalities (Klein et al., 2007; 2013; Salgado et al., 2003), there is renewed interest in exploring bacteriophage genomes to discover new antimicrobial agents.
evidence: Statement about current research trends supported by citations.

claim: Antibiotics currently on the market do not target bacterial DNA replication components directly.
source: Although bacterial DNA replication proteins are strikingly distinct from those found in eukaryotes and archaea (Leipe et al., 1999), antibiotics currently on the market do not target replication components directly, suggesting that this system may be a valuable prospective drug target (McHenry, 2011; Robinson et al., 2010; 2012).
evidence: Statement about current antibiotic targets supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial DNA replication may be a valuable prospective drug target.
source: Although bacterial DNA replication proteins are strikingly distinct from those found in eukaryotes and archaea (Leipe et al., 1999), antibiotics currently on the market do not target replication components directly, suggesting that this system may be a valuable prospective drug target (McHenry, 2011; Robinson et al., 2010; 2012).
evidence: Speculative statement based on current knowledge and citations.

claim: 77ORF104 could act at multiple stages during the DNA replication cycle where helicase-loading events are utilized, including both initiation and replication restart.
source: This result indicates that 77ORF104 could in principle act at multiple stages during the DNA replication cycle where helicase-loading events are utilized, including both initiation and replication restart (Bell and Kaguni, 2013; Heller and Marians, 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the finding that 77ORF104 does not disrupt helicase-loader interactions.

claim: The ISM is a specialized feature that phylogenetically distinguishes helicase loaders and bacterial replication initiator proteins from other AAA+ superfamily members.
source: Within AAA+ ATPases, one specialized feature that phylogenetically distinguishes helicase loaders such as DnaI and bacterial replication initiator proteins from other superfamily members is the existence of an extra α-helix that is inserted into one edge of the core AAA+ fold (Iyer et al., 2004). This element, termed the Initiator/loader-Specific Motif (ISM) (Dueber et al., 2007)
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ISM has been shown to be important for self-assembly and function in replicative helicase loaders and initiators.
source: This element, termed the Initiator/loader-Specific Motif (ISM) (Dueber et al., 2007), has been shown to be important for self-assembly and function in replicative helicase loaders and initiators (Mott et al., 2008; Dueber et al., 2007; Erzberger et al., 2006; Duderstadt et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In nucleotide-oligomerized DnaA and DnaC/I structures, the ISM introduces a significant out-of-plane displacement of adjacent ATPase folds.
source: In nucleotide-oligomerized DnaA and DnaC/I structures, the ISM introduces a significant out-of-plane displacement of adjacent ATPase folds, and appears responsible for pushing these assemblies into a helical, as opposed to closed-ring, formation.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of DnaA and DnaC/I.

claim: The conformational change in the SaDnaI ISM is not the result of crystal packing interactions.
source: Examination of the crystal contacts in our SaDnaIAAA+•77ORF104 structure indicates that the change in conformation of the ISM is not the result of packing interactions, indicating that binding of the 77ORF104 inhibitor is responsible for introducing this conformational change in SaDnaIAAA+.
evidence: Based on analysis of crystal contacts in the structure.

claim: Bacterial helicase loaders typically require helicase binding and/or ssDNA binding to promote ATPase activity.
source: Previous studies of Bacillus subtilis DnaI and the related E. coli DnaC protein have shown that bacterial helicase loaders typically require helicase binding and/or ssDNA binding to promote ATPase activity (Ioannou et al., 2006; Learn et al., 1997; Davey et al., 2002)
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ATPase activity of bacterial helicase loaders is proposed to directly depend on loader self-assembly.
source: Previous studies of Bacillus subtilis DnaI and the related E. coli DnaC protein have shown that bacterial helicase loaders typically require helicase binding and/or ssDNA binding to promote ATPase activity (Ioannou et al., 2006; Learn et al., 1997; Davey et al., 2002), a function proposed to directly depend on loader self assembly (Mott et al., 2008).
evidence: Proposed mechanism supported by citation.

claim: DnaI ATPase domain constructs containing a portion of the linker crystallized as monomers even in the presence of nucleotide.
source: This observation explains why DnaI ATPase domain constructs containing a portion of the linker crystallized as monomers even in the presence of nucleotide
evidence: Observation from crystallization experiments.

claim: SaDnaI forms visible microcrystals when chilled on ice at elevated concentrations that can be sedimented after brief centrifugation.
source: When chilled on ice at elevated concentrations, SaDnaI oligomerizes into visible microcrystals that can be sedimented after a brief centrifugation step.
evidence: Observation from pelleting assays described in supplemental information.

claim: 77ORF104 keeps SaDnaI in solution and prevents pelleting.
source: In line with our predictions, the loader remains in solution when incubated with the inhibitor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: On its own, SaDnaI forms a very broad, polydisperse mixture of species with a large average molecular weight as measured by dynamic light scattering.
source: The resultant data show that on its own, SaDnaI forms a very broad, polydisperse mixture of species with a large average molecular weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: When measured in the presence of 77ORF104, SaDnaI forms a much smaller, less polydisperse species.
source: By contrast, when measured in the presence of the inhibitor protein, a much smaller, less polydisperse species is formed.
evidence: Supported by dynamic light scattering data.

claim: The SaDnaC helicase associates with both the SaDnaI helicase loader and the phage helicase loader homolog 77ORF013.
source: The data from this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) show that: 1) the SaDnaC helicase associates with both the SaDnaI helicase loader and the phage helicase loader homolog 77ORF013
evidence: Supported by analytical gel filtration data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibitor 77ORF104 does not affect the migration of either the SaDnaI helicase loader or phage loader 77ORF013 or the SaDnaC helicase in analytical gel filtration.
source: The data from this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) show that: 1) the SaDnaC helicase associates with both the SaDnaI helicase loader and the phage helicase loader homolog 77ORF013 (albeit with a degree of instability, as the bands for the helicase and loader proteins do not perfectly overlap –the peak maxima for ORF013 alone occurs at fraction 44 and for ORF013 plus SaDnaI at fraction 42, and at fractions 42 and 40 for SaDnaI alone and with SaDnaC, respectively), and 2) that the inhibitor does not affect the migration of either the SaDnaI helicase loader or phage loader 77ORF013 or the SaDnaC helicase.
evidence: Supported by analytical gel filtration data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The S. aureus helicase SaDnaC does not appear to form a stable homo-hexameric ring but instead migrates as an apparent dimeric species.
source: Interestingly, based on standards run on the same column (not shown), the helicase SaDnaC does not appear to form a stable homo-hexameric ring but instead migrates as an apparent dimeric species.
evidence: Inferred from analytical gel filtration data.

claim: In B. subtilis, helicase loading occurs by a DnaI-directed assembly process rather than by a ring opening mechanism.
source: In B. subtilis, helicase loading has been reported to occur not by a ring opening mechanism (as is thought to happen in E. coli) (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Davey and O'Donnell, 2003), but rather by a DnaI-directed assembly process that additionally requires two co-chaperones not found in Gram-negative organisms, DnaB (which is unrelated to the E. coli DnaB helicase) and DnaD (Rokop et al., 2004; Smits et al., 2010; Velten et al., 2003).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Stable hexamers have been observed for Gram-positive DnaC helicases, but only when using thermophilic proteins.
source: Stable hexamers have been observed for Gram-positive DnaC helicases, but only when using thermophilic proteins (e.g. B. stearothermophilus and G. kaustophilus [Bailey et al., 2007a; Ioannou et al., 2006; Lo et al., 2009; Soultanas, 2002; Tsai et al., 2009b]), whose room-temperature behavior may differ from their mesophilic counterparts.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dimers of DnaB-family helicases have been observed previously, wherein the dimer is stabilized by interactions between the N-terminal 'collar' domains of the protein.
source: It should be noted that dimers of DnaB-family helicases have been observed previously, wherein the dimer is stabilized by interactions between the N-terminal 'collar' domains of the protein (Bailey et al., 2007b).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: S. aureus helicase/loader interactions form but are somewhat unstable.
source: Our findings, which show that S. aureus helicase/loader interactions form but are somewhat unstable, and that the DnaC helicase does not readily assemble a pre-formed hexamer, are in accord with observations reported for the B. subtilis system.
evidence: Inferred from analytical gel filtration data.
